source: MacGregor, Ormerod, Chronicle (2001) Information processing and insight: a process model of performance on the nine-dot and related problems
finding: Founding paper. Model of nine-dot difficulty built on maximization and progress-monitoring heuristics with lookahead. Five experiments. The authors say insight problem solving can be modelled inside a means-ends analysis frame.
numbers: Experiments 1 and 2: model predicted performance on nine-dot and related problems. Experiment 3: extension accounts for insightful moves. Experiments 4 and 5: critical test of model against earlier accounts. No sample sizes seen.
quote: Maximization and progress-monitoring heuristics are the source of problem difficulty, but also create the conditions necessary for insightful moves to be sought.
limits: Abstract only (OpenAlex record). Full text not open. All MacGregor 2001 numbers below are second-hand from papers that cite it.
agent_relevance: Difficulty and the trigger for change come from the same loop: greedy progress, then a code-checkable failure to meet a progress criterion.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (theory section)
finding: Statement of the criterion-of-satisfactory-progress (CSP) theory. Solvers pick moves that look like the most progress toward goal properties inferred from the problem text. A move is judged against a criterion. When no move meets it, the solver relaxes the demand to maximize. A non-maximal move that leads to later gain is kept as a promising state.
numbers: Nine-dot criterion: dots remaining divided by lines remaining; at the start 9/4 = 2.25 dots per line, so a line through 3 dots passes. Six-coin criterion: (goal coins on ring - current) / moves left; first move needs +0.67, 1 in whole coins.
quote: individuals evaluate potential moves against a criterion of satisfactory progress
limits: Criterion is built from goal properties the solver infers, not from a known goal state. Assumes one-move lookahead in the worked example.
agent_relevance: Direct recipe for code: gap = goal measure minus current measure; need = gap / moves left; a move whose gain is below need is criterion failure. Cheap to compute when the task has a countable goal property.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 1, ring condition)
finding: Six-coin problem with a ring goal shown. Move choices matched hill-climbing on coins-on-ring. Success rates for first, second and third moves matched the one-lookahead CSP prediction almost exactly.
numbers: N=19 analysed (20 tested, 1 lost). 6 solved in 10 min (32%). 177 first moves, 20 correct (11.3%) vs predicted 11% (random 8.3%). 6 of 20 correct first moves had a correct second (30%) vs predicted 33% (random 4.3%). 6 of 6 then correct third (100%) vs predicted 100%. Predicted attempt success .036; expected solvers 5.5 of 19; chance .00015 gives 0.03 solvers; observed 6, p<.001 binomial.
limits: Single lab, small N. State space: 7426 legal 3-move sequences, 2 reach the ring, 176 a two-group end.
agent_relevance: Shows a progress rule can predict step-by-step success odds on a small puzzle. Good template for a test: predict per-step pass rate from the criterion, compare with logs.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 1, maximization test)
finding: Participants chose first moves that put more coins on the ring than chance. This is the maximization heuristic, and it points away from the solution.
numbers: Mean coins on ring after first move 4.42 vs chance 4.08 (SD 0.49), t(18)=3.02, p<.01. Of 12 distinct first moves: 2 give 5 on ring (meet criterion, entrap a coin, guarantee failure), 9 give 4, 1 gives 3.
limits: Effect is modest in size. Participants with deeper lookahead would reject the maximizing move, so the average mixes lookahead levels.
agent_relevance: Greedy move that passes the progress test can be the trap. The detector must not treat a high progress score as safe; revisit when repeated best-score attempts all dead-end.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 1, abstract goal condition)
finding: When the goal was given only as words (each coin touches exactly two others), most people still pictured a ring and behaved as if hill-climbing toward it. They did not find the ring solution and found the two-group solution no more than chance.
numbers: N=19 analysed. 74% said they inferred a ring goal. 0 ring solutions in Abstract vs 6 in Ring (Fisher p<.01). Two-group solution 5 of 19 (26%) vs chance expectation 2.2 (2.6 on non-solver attempts); binomial test not significant, power .38. Final states with separated coins 4.8% (6 of 124) vs 16.1% of all possible end states, chi2=11.68.
limits: Low power. Chance-level two-group finds could be luck. Chunk-avoidance (not splitting a figure) is not ruled out here; Experiment 2 tests it.
agent_relevance: Agents infer goal properties from text and then climb toward them. A code step can list the goal properties the model assumed and test if the progress criterion is built on an inferred, unchecked property.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 2)
finding: Starting layout that looks like a partial ring made the two-group solution harder than a straight-line start, though both are 2-move solvable. This supports the idea that the inferred ring goal blocks search elsewhere.
numbers: N=54 high-school visitors, 27 per condition (inferred from equal split). Partial-ring 4 solved (15%) vs straight-line 11 (41%), chi2(1,54)=4.52, p<.05. Straight-line 11 vs chance 2.1, p<.001; partial-ring 4 vs chance 2.8 not significant. 3 min limit.
limits: Group-setting test; attempts not recorded. Chance estimates borrowed from Experiment 1 attempt rates.
agent_relevance: Cues that strengthen a wrong goal picture lower success. Remove or vary the goal framing when stuck.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 3)
finding: Showing the two-group solution almost always led to its reproduction; showing the ring example did not help and slowed the search. Difficulty is about which goal is held, not about drawing skill.
numbers: N=42. Two-group solvers: Abstract 3 (27%), Ring-example 3 (27%), Two-group example 8 (89%), Both examples 10 (91%); chi2(3,42)=16.84, p<.015. Attempts: facilitation by two-group example F(1,20)=18.08 p<.001; inhibition by ring example F(1,20)=6.92 p<.02. 8 of 11 Abstract participants (73%) reported a ring goal.
limits: Hex tokens used for easier contact counting. Small cells.
agent_relevance: A shown example of the wrong goal slows exploration. When an agent has a goal exemplar, check that it is not narrowing search.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (Experiment 4, six-coin vs ten-coin)
finding: Ten-coin triangle, a classic insight problem, was solved far more than the six-coin problem. The authors say CSP predicts this because the hill-climbing move choice sits closer to the correct path in the ten-coin problem. Restructuring accounts would not predict the ten-coin to be easier.
numbers: N=48 analysed (50 tested). First-attempt solve: six-coin 0 (0%), ten-coin 9 (19%), Wilcoxon z=2.65, p=.008. Within 5 min: six-coin 10 (20.8%), ten-coin 36 (75%), z=2.67, p=.008. Standard ten-coin instructions gave 65% in the same time.
limits: Post-hoc argument for why ten-coin is easier; chance solve probabilities were close (.00041 vs .00015). Within-subject order effects handled by counterbalancing.
agent_relevance: Problem difficulty can be predicted from the pattern of moves that pass the progress test and sit on the solution path. This is a way to forecast which items need an impasse-breaking step.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (recoding, Experiments 1 and 3)
finding: Solvers often could not reproduce a ring solution right after finding it or after seeing it demonstrated. Two-group solvers reproduced easily. The authors argue some insight feel comes from recoding a solution after the fact.
numbers: Exp 1: of 6 ring solvers, 2 reproduced within 1 min. 6 of 19 Abstract participants reproduced after demonstration plus 6 min filler; 13 failed, of whom 6 failed again after a second demo, 1 of 5 succeeded after a third. Of 14 who reproduced, 5 (36%) failed with the start reversed. Exp 3: 7 of 36 (19%) reproduced the ring after seeing it.
limits: Memory for move sequences, not direct evidence on progress monitoring.
agent_relevance: A found solution should be stored as a verified program or structure, not as a remembered path.

source: Chronicle, MacGregor, Ormerod (2004) What makes an insight problem? Roles of heuristics, goal conception and solution recoding in knowledge-lean problems (framing: Weisberg classification)
finding: Review of what counts as an insight problem. Weisberg (1996) sorted 24 problems: 4 discontinuity-only (e.g. anagrams), 5 hybrid (e.g. nine-dot), 15 pure insight (e.g. matchsticks). CSP is placed in the process-based camp that sees insight and non-insight as alike.
numbers: 24 problems: 4 / 5 / 15.
limits: Secondhand summary of Weisberg 1996.
agent_relevance: Our schema should not assume impasses need special insight machinery; a progress rule may cover both.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor, Chronicle (2002) Dynamics and constraints in insight problem solving
finding: Eight-coin problem. Starting layouts that offer many moves bringing a coin to touch three others (strategic moves) lower solution rates, since these moves look like progress but guarantee failure. Visual hints about the right first move were ignored when such strategic moves were available.
numbers: Two experiments. Abstract page read only; no numbers on the page.
quote: a full account of insight problem solving must incorporate a dynamic that steers solution-seeking activity toward the constraints
limits: Abstract page of repository read; full text not open. Numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Attractive local moves block hints. A prompt hint will often be ignored if the agent has a high-scoring move already. Require failure of the passing moves before a hint is used.

source: Chronicle, Ormerod, MacGregor (2001) When insight just won't come: the failure of visual cues in the nine-dot problem
finding: Visual and verbal hints to leave the dot square gave little or no gain. Practice drawing the solution shape did not transfer to the plain nine-dot problem, which stayed at floor. Argues against pure Gestalt shape mismatch.
numbers: Three experiments. Abstract page read only; shading cue gave minimal improvement, shading plus a relevance hint gave modest, not significant, gains; both verbal and visual hints together improved performance only slightly; transfer task at floor.
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not given there. Authors say visual constraint relaxation is unlikely to be the sole process.
agent_relevance: Telling a model what the escape is does not suffice; progress criterion must also be met.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem
finding: Competing account to CSP built from nine-dot variants. Reports the four principles of the MacGregor theory and says its lookahead story gives the same shallow explanation as older theories. Proposes a disposition to turn only on dots (and not to cross lines) as the main constraint.
numbers: States MacGregor et al. principles: (a) draw each line through as many dots as possible; (b) value a line by dots picked up relative to dots left and lines left; (c) lookahead 1 to 4; (d) if every line leads to insufficient progress, consider lines outside the figure with some probability. Cites solve rate under 5% for undergraduates given a few minutes.
quote: people look ahead 1, 2, 3 or at most 4 steps when deciding which line to draw next
limits: Secondary description of the theory by competing authors.
agent_relevance: Clear four-rule spec that can be coded as a simulator.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (Experiment, N=90)
finding: Training on non-dot turns raised solution of a nine-dot variant. Training meant to harden the constraints did not lower it.
numbers: N=90, 30 per group. First insight variant solved: facilitating 19 (63%), hindering 8 (27%), none 11 (37%), chi2(2,N=90)=8.836, p<.05. Facilitating vs hindering chi2(1,60)=8.148; vs none 4.267; hindering vs none .693 ns. Mean time 116 s, 188 s, 185 s, F(2,87)=5.873. 4 min per problem.
limits: Floor effect likely for hindering. Conference paper, uncorrected multiple tests.
agent_relevance: Training a missing move type works more than hinting; suggests offering a specific operator, not generic exhortation.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2001) Training for insight: the case of the nine-dot problem (completion split)
finding: Within the facilitating group, only those who completed training correctly benefited.
numbers: 19 completed (at least 6 of 12 correct): 17 solved (89%). 11 did not complete: 2 solved (18%). chi2(1,N=30)=15.248, p<.05.
limits: Post-hoc split by training success, so confounded with ability.
agent_relevance: Transfer needs the operator to be mastered before it helps.

source: Ormerod, Chronicle, MacGregor (2001) Facilitation in variants of the nine-dot problem: perceptual or cognitive mediation?
finding: Adding dots that make a good arrow shape made the nine-dot solution easy, even on the first trial. Cognitive accounts (dot-turn constraint, CSP) cannot explain the first-trial gap since all added-dot versions need only dot-to-dot lines. The authors grant a role for perceptual (figural) mediation.
numbers: Exp 1: first-trial solvers 73% (13 dots), 60% (12), 50% (11), 0% (9). After 10 one-minute trials: 90%, 80%, 93%, 0%. Exp 2 with unfilled guide dots: 33% solved after 5 trials. Sample sizes not shown in the 2-page paper.
limits: Two-page conference summary with no N, no test statistics beyond planned comparisons. Authors are CSP authors, so this is a limit they themselves state on CSP.
agent_relevance: Boundary for the progress model: surface layout can steer the first move, so layout cues count even when the progress rule is the same.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter, Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem
finding: Test of the lookahead idea with spatial working memory. In plain nine-dot, higher spatial span went with drawing lines outside the dot square. Verbal span did not.
numbers: Exp 1: N=51 analysed (52 tested). 7 drew outside (14%); 6 of the 7 in the high spatial WM group, chi2(1,N=51)=4.15, p=.04; verbal WM chi2=0.65, p=.42. Spatial WM mean 31.14 (SD 6.06) for the 7 vs 26.24 (SD 5.72), t(49)=1.99, p=.026 one-tailed. Only 5 of 51 solved (about 10%); 5 of the 7 who went outside solved. Spatial WM and solve: chi2=2.13, p=.14, not significant.
limits: Few solvers, low power. Spatial span is a proxy for lookahead, not a direct measure. One-tailed tests.
agent_relevance: Support for the claim that plan depth (a resource) limits detecting dead ends early. For an agent, lookahead depth is a settable budget.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter, Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem (Experiment 2)
finding: With a training set and a hint that three lines must extend past the dots, spatial WM predicted who solved. Verbal WM did not.
numbers: N=54 analysed (72 recruited, 14 had seen the problem, 4 incomplete). Point-biserial spatial WM with solving r(52)=.452, p<.001; verbal r(52)=.199, p=.148; difference between dependent correlations t(51)=1.73, p=.046 one-tailed. 10 min.
limits: Training plus hint changes the task, which the authors acknowledge; they argue solved version is still planning-dependent.
agent_relevance: Even after being told the escape, success depends on planning capacity. Hints do not remove the need for lookahead.

source: Chein, Weisberg, Streeter, Kwok (2010) Working memory and insight in the nine-dot problem (framing of the debate)
finding: Explains why the Gestalt reading fails: telling people to go outside the box makes all draw outside the box (Weisberg and Alba 1981) but only a small minority solve. Kershaw and Ohlsson 2004 found modest gains from single-factor aids and large gains only from combined aids. Lavric et al. 2000 and Fleck 2008 found no WM role in insight problems, which the authors dispute for nine-dot.
numbers: Nine-dot: very few naive solvers even with 100 attempts (Weisberg and Alba 1981). Chronicle et al. 2001: computer models with differing lookahead performed as predicted on the nine-dot.
limits: Review text of a participant in the debate.
agent_relevance: Supports multi-cause difficulty. Our schema should combine detection of impasse with several remedies, not one.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (theory statement)
finding: Frames progress monitoring as: insight is sought only when the distance to goal cannot be closed in the moves left (criterion failure). For nine-dot, criterion failure arrives only at the fourth line, too late; deeper lookahead brings it earlier. Names the problem for unlimited-move tasks: no fixed move count, so the criterion cannot be computed.
numbers: Lookahead distribution from MacGregor et al. 2001: 32% lookahead one, 32% two, 36% three. Criterion for nine-dot about 2.25 dots per line. A diagonal given first line is predicted to be a better aid than a horizontal outward line because it forces search sooner. Nine-dot standard version: nobody solves in 10 min (Burnham and Davis 1969) nor in 100 attempts (Weisberg and Alba 1981).
quote: insight is only sought once it becomes apparent that the distance to the goal is unachievable in the moves remaining
limits: Describes MacGregor model secondhand.
agent_relevance: Two key limits: needs a move budget, needs a distance measure. Our code-side detector must supply both or use a surrogate.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (method)
finding: Car park (Rush Hour type) insight problem solved by moving the taxi first. Impasse defined by eye fixation time on a move at or above that participant's mean plus 2 SD.
numbers: N=39 psychology undergraduates, 13 per condition (normal, rotated 90 degrees, easy practice). Four practice problems before the insight item. Eye tracker at 50 Hz. 37 had usable eye data. 8 needed a hint and are counted as non-solvers (6 normal, 1 rotated, 1 easy); 31 solved unaided.
limits: Small sample, one task. Impasse threshold chosen by the author.
agent_relevance: A concrete, per-person, per-move impasse rule (mean + 2 SD of own move time) that code can apply to logs.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (progress monitoring result)
finding: Participants were sorted into lookahead groups by where their longest impasses fell. Deeper-lookahead people (impasse early) solved faster, in fewer moves, and all solved.
numbers: By time in impasse: 20 (54%) lookahead one or two, 11 (30%) lookahead three (predicted 64%/36%); by raw impasse counts the fit was worse. Table 2: solvers 14 vs 11; non-solvers 6 vs 0; moves to solution 37.14 vs 21.36; time 92.29 s vs 42.73 s. Solvers faster F(1,23)=26.81, p<.001; fewer moves F(1,23)=10.94, p<.01.
limits: Lookahead is inferred from the same impasse data used for the outcome, which makes the test partly circular. Non-solvers excluded from time analyses.
agent_relevance: Early recognition of a dead end predicts success. Count time spent stalled, not the number of stalls.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (head-to-head test)
finding: Representational change predicted success rates better than progress monitoring in the manipulations. Easy practice and a rotated board both raised solving, which PM predicts should not change anything.
numbers: Solvers (unaided): normal 7 of 13, rotated 12 of 13, easy 12 of 13 (derived from 31 total and hint counts; the source table is garbled). Normal vs rotated/easy combined: Fisher exact p=.01. Erroneous clicks, U=76, N=39, p<.01. No difference in moves or time among solvers (F(1,29)=1.56 and 1.90).
limits: Counts reconstructed from a garbled PDF table; check against the published version. Predictions for opposing theories drawn by the same author. Non-intuitive result needs replication.
agent_relevance: Context shapes the starting representation. A fresh restart with a changed problem layout can help when progress logs show a stall.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (representational change impasse findings)
finding: All solvers hit an impasse before the taxi move; 5 right before it. Non-solvers: 3 never moved the taxi; 5 moved it but put it back. Solvers looked at the key region more during the relevant impasse.
numbers: 37 analysable: 30 solvers, 7 non-solvers. Solver fixation share on the right 12 squares 24% vs non-solver 9% (F(1,39)=6.50, p<.05); time share 19% vs 8% (F(1,39)=5.56, p<.05). Taxi move longer than 3 moves before and after (fixation F(2,58)=5.40, p<.01).
limits: Eye data quality excluded 2 people. Eye position is attention, not understanding.
agent_relevance: A stall is not enough. Where the effort lands matters. Log which parts of the problem the model re-reads.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (proposal to merge theories)
finding: Author proposes merging: progress monitoring says when alternative search starts; representational change says how it succeeds. Neither alone covers both.
quote: The progress monitoring theory essentially covers insight up to the point at which insight is sought.
limits: Argument, not a tested merged model.
agent_relevance: Matches our split: code-side trigger (progress) plus operators for reframing (relax a constraint, split a chunk).

source: Ormerod, MacGregor, Chronicle, Dewald, Chu (2013) Act first, think later: presence and absence of inferential planning in problem solving
finding: Formal CSP: maximization picks moves, minimization limits the space, a criterion evaluates moves. Lookahead is the count of mentally tested steps; new here is lookahead zero (select the maximizing move without testing). Seven model assumptions. Earlier estimate of nine-dot lookahead: 32%, 32%, 36%, 0% for one, two, three, four.
numbers: Model assumptions listed in Table 1; each lookahead level gives different predicted first moves for 7-, 8-, 9-ball weighing.
limits: Lookahead estimates from nine-dot are reused for other tasks. In the weighing task zero and one lookahead are common because outcomes cannot be seen.
agent_relevance: Gives the minimal algorithm: sample by maximization, test k steps against a criterion, expand space when none pass. Easy to code; k is a tunable knob.

source: Ormerod, MacGregor, Chronicle, Dewald, Chu (2013) Act first, think later: presence and absence of inferential planning in problem solving (Experiment 1 and fit)
finding: Weighing puzzle with two steps. Model fitted first-weigh choices with lookahead estimates from Simmel 1953 (37% zero, 31.5% one or two, 21% three; N=19). Seven-ball easiest, then eight, then nine.
numbers: N=80 undergraduates, 5 min. Solved: 7-ball 9/26 (35%), 8-ball 5/28 (18%), 9-ball 2/26 (8%), chi2(2)=6.01, p=.049. 7-ball 3v3 route 8 (31%) vs 2v2 route 1 (4%), Fisher p=.02. Observed vs predicted frequency of 18 weigh categories: r=.96, slope 1.02, intercept -0.08. 37% of nine-ball participants chose the uninformative 5v4 weigh (zero lookahead).
limits: Estimates from Simmel are used to predict the same data type, so part of the fit is circular for nine-ball. Eight-ball vs nine-ball not significant (p=.24).
agent_relevance: Evidence that many people (about 37% here) accept a max-progress move with no check. A model that skips testing a move is the same failure; force a one-step test.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt, Szathmary (2016) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization
finding: Ten-penny problem (5 rows of 4). Relaxing the penny constraint was needed but not enough; adding a maximization hint (draw five lines, each with exactly four intersections) was what raised solving. Direct test of the combined account.
numbers: N=120 (30 per group; 4 groups). Solved: control 3/30 (10%), line hint 2/29 (7%), intersection hint 6/28 (21%), maximization hint 21/29 (72%). Hints after 5 min; 15 min limit. Pennies-only strategy before hint 60%, 59%, 46%, 59%; after hint 33%, 3%, 7%, 0%.
limits: One task; the maximization hint tells the target score, so it turns the task into a check with a number. Denominators vary (29, 28) because of exclusions.
agent_relevance: Strongest result for us. A scalar progress target plus a relaxed constraint beats either alone. In-agent: give a countable goal measure after the representation changes.

source: Oellinger, Fedor, Brodt, Szathmary (2016) Insight into the ten-penny problem: guiding search by constraints and maximization (solver behaviour)
finding: Solvers found promising moves earlier, had higher maximization and variation rates across attempts than non-solvers.
numbers: 47% of solvers (15) used intersections before the 5 min hint vs 26% of non-solvers (22). Effect statistics for maximization score and variation score reported in text.
limits: Correlational; solvers may differ in ability.
agent_relevance: Candidates for cheap code-side signals: how often attempts change (variation) and how often the best score improves.

source: Spiridonov, Loginov, Ivanchei, Kurgansky (2019) The role of motor activity in insight problem solving (nine-dot)
finding: Tablet drawing study of nine-dot. Summarises MacGregor model as maximization and progress-monitoring heuristics with lookahead 1 to 4. Argues model needs an account of how lines start outside the square; adds on-line planning (movement-linked) to off-line lookahead.
numbers: Exp 1: 52.8% solved (19 solvers, 17 non-solvers analysed). Exp 2: N=64, solution 37.5% after dot-turn training vs 78.1% after non-dot-turn training, chi2(1,N=64)=10.83, p=.001; overall 57.8%. Exp 2 non-dot-turn effect on movement time F(1,61)=7.8, p=.007. Cites MacGregor 2001 Exp 1: 80 to 93% solved on simplified problems while no one solved the nine-dot.
limits: Read the introduction, methods and results lines of the PDF text; not every table. High solve rates reflect training that gave the key operator.
agent_relevance: Shows that the model alone needs a supplement for how the escape move is generated.

source: Oellinger, Jones, Faber, Knoblich (2013) Cognitive mechanisms of insight: role of heuristics and representational change in solving the eight-coin problem
finding: Tested the CSP account of the eight-coin problem against grouping and constraint accounts with six new versions. Two sources of difficulty: the 2D constraint and perceptual groupings. Move analysis said selection was driven by the established representation, not by the heuristics.
numbers: Six new versions of eight-coin; no numbers seen.
limits: Abstract only (OpenAlex). Competing explanation to CSP.
agent_relevance: Boundary of the progress account: representation fixes which moves are even sampled.

source: Kershaw and Ohlsson (2004) Multiple causes of difficulty in insight: the case of the nine-dot problem
finding: Three experiments: nine-dot difficulty has several causes in perception, knowledge and process. Removing one cause moves solution rates only a little.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Abstract only (OpenAlex). Cited with numbers in Chein et al. 2010.
agent_relevance: Supports combining several remedies.

source: Ormerod (2024) How many heuristics are enough? Testing a parsimonious theory of possibility generation in problem-solving (PRODIGI)
finding: Per a search summary, a newer model PRODIGI is argued to replace the earlier criterion-of-satisfactory-progress account, and the paper questions whether Jones 2003 discriminated between the models. Also says solvers run at lookahead one, two or three, about a third each.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Not opened. Publisher page blocked. Claims come from a search-engine summary only; treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Follow-up to open in the next pass; may change the model the detector is based on.
